Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN)  -- Bolivian officials have declared a health emergency after three deaths attributed to dengue hemorrhagic fever, the often-lethal form of a mosquito-borne disease that more than 1,000 Bolivians are thought to have contracted since November. Brazilian soldiers pour insecticide to fight dengue fever in 2008. Bolivia also is battling the mosquito-borne disease. At least 12 unconfirmed instances of dengue hemorrhagic fever have been reported in the first 17 days of 2009, the official ABI news agency said. About 250 cases of dengue fever, the milder, nonlethal form of the disease, have been confirmed in the past two weeks, said Health Minister Ramiro Tapia in the Los Tiempos de Cochabamba newspaper. Authorities said they have committed more than 20,000 military personnel and 2.5 tons of insecticide to combat the disease. A preteen boy died last week at Children's Hospital of La Paz, a few days after arriving with internal bleeding, hospital director Christian Fuentes told La Razon newspaper in La Paz, the nation's capital. "By that time, there was nothing we could do. He had multiple internal hemorrhages," Fuentes said. A 17-year-old boy and a 30-year-old woman also died last week, the ABI news agency said, citing the national director of epidemiology, Juan Carlos Arraya. Cases of dengue fever usually spike from November through January, which is Bolivia's hot and rainy season. Alberto Nogales, the country's vice minister of health, said the fight against mosquitoes will last until April. Dengue occurs in tropical and subtropical parts of the world, transmitted by the bite of a mosquito infected with one of four dengue viruses, the World Health Organization says. Symptoms, which appear three to 14 days after the bite, can include mild to high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and a rash, the WHO says. Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a potentially fatal complication that affects mainly children, the WHO says. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, vomiting and bleeding. The disease cannot be transmitted directly from one person to another. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there are up to 100 million cases worldwide each year. "It actually is quite common," Dr. Ali Khan of the CDC told CNN last year. "And unfortunately, over the last 30 years or so we've seen an increase in the number of countries infected with dengue fever." Khan attributes the increase in part to population growth. Mosquitoes that carry dengue typically breed in areas near humans. "This is a disease that occurs where there's lots of population," he said. The WHO says mosquitoes carrying dengue viruses breed in exposed water, including places as shallow as jars, discarded bottles and plant saucers. Last year, 55,000 people in southeastern Brazil contracted the disease. The outbreak was confirmed as causing the deaths of at least 67 people -- almost half of them children under 13 -- and another 58 deaths were under investigation last summer, the Rio de Janeiro state's ministry of health reported at the time. Final statistics on the outbreak were not immediately available.

LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN) — Bolivia has put a health emergency in place following three deaths linked to dengue hemorrhagic fever, the frequently deadly version of a mosquito-transmitted illness that officials believe has infected more than 1,000 people in the country since November.

In 2008, Brazilian troops were shown applying insecticide as part of efforts to control dengue fever. Bolivia is now facing its own battle against the same mosquito-borne disease.

During the first 17 days of 2009, at least 12 suspected cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever were reported, according to the state-run ABI news agency. Health Minister Ramiro Tapia told the newspaper *Los Tiempos de Cochabamba* that roughly 250 cases of ordinary dengue fever — the less severe and nonfatal form — had been confirmed over the previous two weeks.

Officials said more than 20,000 members of the military and 2.5 tons of insecticide had been assigned to the campaign to stop the illness from spreading.

Christian Fuentes, director of Children’s Hospital in La Paz, told the newspaper *La Razon* that a boy under the age of 13 died there last week, several days after he was admitted with internal bleeding.

“By that time, there was nothing we could do. He had multiple internal hemorrhages,” Fuentes said.

ABI, citing national epidemiology director Juan Carlos Arraya, reported that two other people — a 17-year-old boy and a 30-year-old woman — also died last week.

Dengue infections in Bolivia generally rise between November and January, the country’s hot, rainy period. Vice Health Minister Alberto Nogales said anti-mosquito operations would continue through April.

According to the World Health Organization, dengue is found in tropical and subtropical regions and spreads when a person is bitten by a mosquito carrying one of the four dengue viruses. The WHO says symptoms typically begin three to 14 days after infection and may include a mild to high fever, intense headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint aches, and a skin rash.

The WHO describes dengue hemorrhagic fever as a dangerous complication that can be fatal and most often affects children. Its symptoms can include fever, stomach pain, vomiting, and bleeding. The illness does not spread directly from person to person.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that as many as 100 million dengue cases occur around the world each year.

“It actually is quite common,” Dr. Ali Khan of the CDC told CNN last year. “And unfortunately, over the last 30 years or so we’ve seen an increase in the number of countries infected with dengue fever.”

Khan said population growth is one factor contributing to that rise. The mosquitoes that transmit dengue usually reproduce in places close to where people live.

“This is a disease that occurs where there’s lots of population,” he said.

The WHO says dengue-carrying mosquitoes lay eggs in uncovered water sources, including very small collections of water in containers such as jars, thrown-away bottles, and saucers under plants.

The previous year, 55,000 people in southeastern Brazil became ill with dengue. Health officials in Rio de Janeiro state said at the time that the outbreak had been confirmed as the cause of at least 67 deaths, nearly half of them among children younger than 13. Another 58 deaths were still being investigated during the summer. Final figures from that outbreak were not immediately available.

**Bolivia declares health emergency as dengue deaths rise**

*La Paz, Bolivia — January 2009*

Bolivia has declared a national health emergency after a sharp rise in dengue fever cases, including deaths from the potentially fatal hemorrhagic form of the disease, government health officials said.

At least **18 people have died** from dengue hemorrhagic fever, and authorities have reported **tens of thousands of suspected dengue cases** across the country, with the eastern department of **Santa Cruz** among the hardest-hit areas. Health officials said the outbreak has strained hospitals and prompted urgent efforts to contain the mosquito-borne virus before it spreads further.

The Bolivian government said it would mobilize additional medical teams, increase surveillance, and expand fumigation campaigns aimed at eliminating breeding sites for the **Aedes aegypti** mosquito, which transmits dengue. Authorities also called on residents to remove standing water from homes, yards, tires and containers, where mosquitoes can breed.

Officials said emergency measures include reinforcing hospitals in affected regions, distributing supplies, and coordinating with local governments to intensify vector-control efforts. In some areas, soldiers and public workers have been deployed to assist with cleanup and spraying operations.

Dengue fever is common in tropical and subtropical regions, but health authorities warned that the hemorrhagic form can become life-threatening. According to the **World Health Organization**, dengue infection can cause high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, rash and fatigue. Severe dengue — sometimes referred to as dengue hemorrhagic fever — can involve bleeding, dangerously low platelet counts, plasma leakage, shock and organ failure.

The **U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** says there is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Care is generally supportive, focusing on fluid management, fever control and close monitoring for warning signs. The CDC advises people with suspected dengue to avoid aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which can increase the risk of bleeding, and to seek medical care if severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy or difficulty breathing occurs.

Bolivia’s emergency comes less than a year after Brazil faced one of the region’s most serious dengue outbreaks. In **2008**, Brazil reported **hundreds of thousands of dengue cases**, with Rio de Janeiro state hit particularly hard. Brazilian authorities recorded more than **100,000 cases in Rio de Janeiro alone** during that outbreak, along with scores of deaths, many involving children.

Public health specialists say the outbreaks underscore the difficulty of controlling dengue in fast-growing urban areas where poor sanitation, water storage, rainy weather and inadequate mosquito control can help the virus spread.

Bolivian officials said the priority is to reduce mosquito populations quickly and prevent more cases of severe dengue.

“We are facing a serious public health situation,” health authorities said, urging communities to cooperate with cleanup campaigns and seek medical attention early if symptoms appear.

**Bolivian officials battle dengue hemorrhagic fever as rainy season fuels mosquito surge**

**LA PAZ, Bolivia** — Bolivian health authorities are stepping up mosquito-control campaigns and expanding hospital readiness as the rainy season drives a rise in dengue infections, including severe cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever, officials said.

Heavy rains across parts of the country have left pools of standing water in neighborhoods, markets and rural communities — ideal breeding sites for *Aedes aegypti*, the mosquito that transmits dengue, Zika and chikungunya. Health workers have been going door to door urging families to eliminate stagnant water, cover water tanks and seek care quickly if symptoms worsen.

“We are seeing the impact of the rainy season in real time,” a senior health official said during a briefing. “The most important thing residents can do is remove containers that collect water and come to a clinic early if they develop warning signs.”

Dengue is a viral illness common in tropical and subtropical regions. Most infections cause flu-like symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, rash and fatigue. But some cases progress to severe dengue — historically called dengue hemorrhagic fever — which can cause bleeding, plasma leakage, shock, organ impairment and death if not treated promptly.

At hospitals in affected regions, staff said emergency rooms are monitoring patients closely for signs of deterioration, particularly children, older adults and people with underlying health problems.

“We can stabilize many patients if they arrive in time,” said a physician at a public hospital in eastern Bolivia. “What worries us are patients who stay home until they have persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding gums or extreme weakness. Those are danger signs.”

There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Care focuses on fluids, fever control and close monitoring. Health officials warn people with suspected dengue to avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, which can increase the risk of bleeding, and to use acetaminophen/paracetamol only as directed.

Authorities have deployed fumigation crews in high-risk areas, but officials emphasized that spraying alone cannot stop transmission. The *Aedes* mosquito often breeds in small amounts of clean water found in buckets, discarded tires, flowerpots, bottle caps and uncovered storage containers.

“Fumigation helps reduce adult mosquitoes, but the eggs and larvae remain if homes and patios are not cleaned,” a municipal health worker said. “Community participation is the decisive factor.”

Dengue outbreaks often intensify during and after periods of rain because mosquito populations expand. Public health experts say urban crowding, inconsistent water storage, inadequate drainage and warmer temperatures can all increase transmission.

Bolivia has faced repeated dengue outbreaks in recent years, especially in warmer lowland departments. Officials said surveillance teams are tracking suspected cases, laboratory confirmations and hospital capacity while coordinating with local governments on cleanup drives.

Health authorities urged residents to seek medical attention immediately if fever is accompanied by warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding, drowsiness, restlessness, cold or clammy skin, or a sudden drop in temperature after several days of fever.

“Dengue can change quickly,” the hospital physician said. “Early evaluation saves lives.”
